openers.acidity-alkalinity-and-salinity: A soil can turn sour, salty or sodic, and each change reshapes what will grow in it. Acidification is the build-up of hydrogen cations that lowers a soil's pH, and rain made acid by air pollutants or ammonium-based fertilizers can drive it fast. Salinity, a soil's salt content, climbs in irrigated fields because nearly all water carries dissolved salts that stay behind in the root zone, and it climbs in unirrigated landscapes too, as across much of Australia. Where sodium predominates among the cations, a different trouble begins, and an index built from sodium, calcium and magnesium helps manage it. Along the way come hard crusts of precipitated minerals and waterlogged soils that hide iron sulfide minerals.

soil-chem-008.title: Salt in the soil, and how it gathers
soil-chem-008.text: Egypt's Aswan High Dam was built in 1970. Afterward, a persistently high water table salinized farmland. Soil salinity is the salt content of a soil, and salinization is the process that raises it. A handful of ions do the work: sodium (Na+), potassium (K+), calcium (Ca2+), magnesium (Mg2+) and chloride (Cl−). Salts arrive through {{ref:soil-found-052}}, in dust and in precipitation. With enough rain they are leached away. Under intense evaporation they rise instead by capillarity and gather near the surface. That is why salts accumulate naturally in dry regions, as across large parts of Australia. People add to the load with irrigation, road salt and disrupted drainage. Growing dryness from human-induced global warming also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils. Salinity seriously degrades land. It harms plant growth and yield, damages roads, bricks, pipes and cables, and degrades water quality. The usual cure is to leach salts out with extra good-quality irrigation water, combined with water-table control and drainage from below. Calcium helps as well, easing effects such as plants' reduced water uptake.

soil-chem-001.title: How soils turn sour over time
soil-chem-001.text: Acid soils begin with lichens and algae. As they break down bare rock surfaces, acidification starts, and with time and weathering soils in natural ecosystems grow more acidic. Soil acidification is the build-up of hydrogen cations in a soil, which lowers its pH. It follows two routes. One adds a proton donor: an acid such as nitric, sulfuric or carbonic acid, or a compound such as aluminium sulfate that releases protons in the soil. The other removes base cations such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium by leaching. Soils on parent materials low in basic cations start out acid and stay that way. {{ref:soil-chem-002}}, agriculture and pollution speed the process up. The costs are real: fewer available nutrients, more toxic elements and weaker biological functions such as {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Acidification is not always harmful, since it helps alkaline soils. It degrades land when it cuts crop productivity and biological activity and leaves soil more open to contamination and erosion. It is most common in Southeast Asia, the Amazon Rainforest, Sub-Saharan Africa and the Eastern United States, each with its own causes. Spreading lime on the surface, covered in {{ref:soil-fert-055}}, can prevent it, as can less fertilizer and irrigation.

soil-chem-010.title: How watering a field can salt it
soil-chem-010.text: Even good water brings salt. Water holding just 0.3 g/L, applied at a modest 10,000 m3/ha a year, delivers 3,000 kg of salt to every hectare each year. Most irrigation water is saltier and applied more heavily, so irrigated areas often receive more than 3,000 kg/ha a year, some as much as 10,000 kg/ha. This is irrigation salinity, the irrigated form of {{ref:soil-chem-008}}. Nearly all water carries dissolved salts, and when plants use the water, the salts stay behind in the root zone. Salinization occurs where evaporation concentrates them faster than drainage flushes them away. Poor drainage and saline irrigation water greatly increase it. In cities it often stems from watering gardens and recreation areas with salt-laden reclaimed water, combined with groundwater processes. Waterlogging is the secondary cause. Irrigation is at most about 70% efficient, so 30% or more of the water goes underground. The water table rises and blocks leaching. Good management prevents the problem by supplying enough drainage water to leach the added salts. Water applied beyond the plants' needs to carry salts away is called the leaching fraction.

soil-chem-011.title: Flushing salt out to keep irrigated fields alive
soil-chem-011.text: About 62 million hectares, 20% of the world's irrigated land, is salt-affected, up from 45 million in the early 1990s. Irrigation is the main human cause, since river water and groundwater carry salts that stay in the soil after the water evaporates. Soil salinity control means preventing that build-up and reclaiming soils already saline. The main method lets 10–20% of the irrigation water leach the soil and leave through a drainage system. Where salinity is stable, drainage water is normally 5 to 10 times saltier than the irrigation water, so salt export matches salt import. During reclamation it may at first be 50 times saltier. After one or two years a new, favorable equilibrium is reached. The stakes are high. In the Indo-Gangetic Plain, yield losses on salt-affected land could be 40% for wheat, 45% for rice, 48% for sugarcane and 63% for cotton. Salinization normally affects 20% to 30% of the land in irrigation projects, and depressions in undulating land degrade most. Salty drainage water can harm areas downstream, so drainage is best limited to wet seasons where possible.

soil-chem-009.title: Sodic soils, where sodium rules the clay
soil-chem-009.text: A soil can be acidic, neutral or alkaline and still be crippled by one element. A sodic soil is one in which sodium (Na+) predominates among the exchangeable and dissolved cations, the ions traded through {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. Sodic soils tend to have very poor structure, which limits or prevents water infiltration and drainage. Where clays are saturated with sodium, the soil breaks down easily into fine particles that wash away. Near the surface these soils tend to form columnar peds. They can also accumulate boron and molybdenum in the root zone at levels toxic to plants. Gypsum is the most common compound for reclaiming them. Salt-tolerant plants, the subject of {{ref:soil-chem-045}}, and salt-loving bacteria of the root zone may help. The term is used loosely, often interchangeably with {{ref:soil-chem-019}}, defined as pH above 8.2, exchangeable sodium above 15% of the cation-exchange capacity, or both.

soil-chem-002.title: Acid rain and the soils it soaks through
soil-chem-002.text: Even clean rain is sour. Atmospheric carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, leaving natural rain at around pH 5.0–5.5. Acid rain and snow are more acidic still, and they acidify soil rapidly, mainly through sulfuric and nitric acids formed from air pollutants. Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides come from lightning, volcanoes or human emissions, and react with water in the air to form those stronger acids. Fossil fuels are the largest human source of sulfuric gases, and motor exhaust the largest of nitrogen oxides. As acid rain flows through soil, it leaches calcium and other base cations, and aluminium and proton levels rise. This is {{ref:soil-chem-001}} on a fast clock. Snow brings its own hazard. It holds more nitric than sulfuric acid, so a spring meltwater pulse, up to 50% of annual precipitation, can sharply but briefly lower the pH of drainage water. That drop can release Al3+, which is toxic to fish, especially newly hatched fry. Soils buffer part of the acid. Adsorbing sulfate releases OH−, and organic-rich surface layers in forests cut the H+ load reaching the mineral horizons below. Prevention works. Cutting sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions reduces acid rain and soil acidification, as improving water pH in Ontario lakes showed.

soil-chem-005.title: How fertilizer can sour the ground it feeds
soil-chem-005.text: Most nitrogen fertilizers carry a hidden dose of acid. Fertilizer-induced acidification is the lowering of soil pH by chemical fertilizers, above all ammonium-based nitrogen and sulfur fertilizers. The ammonium-based ones acidify most: ammonium sulfate, diammonium and monoammonium phosphate, and {{ref:soil-fert-071}}. {{ref:soil-fert-021}} and compost acidify less. Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate, do not acidify at all. The reason lies in what happens to ammonium in the soil. As it is converted to nitrate, the process releases hydrogen ions and nitric acid as byproducts, and these keep acidifying the soil. Sulfur fertilizers vary just as widely. Elemental sulfur and iron sulfate can be highly acidifying, while potassium sulfate has no significant effect on pH. Farming systems can magnify the effect. Growing one crop year after year with chemical fertilization often brings acidification and degradation. Under continuous sugarcane, acidity rose, fertility fell and the soil's microbes shifted.

soil-chem-039.title: Duricrust, the hard shell some dry soils wear
soil-chem-039.text: Some soils grow a stone lid. A duricrust is a hard layer on or near the soil surface where soluble minerals have precipitated and hardened. It can be a few millimeters thick or several meters. The general term is not to be confused with duripan. Duricrusts form as mineral-bearing waters move up, down or sideways by capillary action and deposit soluble minerals, often helped by evaporation in arid settings. In the per ascensum model, evaporation draws solutions up from a shallow water table to form thin crusts. In the per descensum model, downward-percolating solutions build thick ones. Each type is named for its dominant mineral. Ferricrete is rich in iron sesquioxides, alcrete in aluminium sesquioxides, silcrete in silica, calcrete in calcium carbonate and gypcrete in gypsum. The same layers go by other names, among them laterite, bauxite, {{ref:soil-chem-036}} and {{ref:soil-chem-038}}. Duricrust found at the Viking 2 and Phoenix landing sites on Mars, the latter confirmed water-based, may help show the planet once had more water.

soil-chem-024.title: Dryland salinity: clear the trees, raise the salt
soil-chem-024.text: Salt can ruin land that has never seen an irrigation ditch. Dryland salinity is salinity in unirrigated landscapes: a rise in the salt of soil, water or the wider environment beyond normal levels. It is natural, but human activity greatly worsens it. It results from groundwater recharge, movement and discharge. Native vegetation forms a 'soil sponge' of roots and soil up to 6 metres deep that keeps the water table low. Shallow-rooted crops such as wheat thin that sponge to 1 metre or less. Once deep-rooted plants are cleared, excess water seeps past the root zone and the water table rises. Capillary action then brings salt to the surface. This happens when the water table is two to three metres down in clayey soils, but less than a metre in sandy ones. Clearing as little as 25% of a catchment can cause salinity. In many Australian landscapes, aquifer capacity is orders of magnitude below the altered recharge. Salts accumulate wherever evaporation outpaces rainfall's replenishment of groundwater, as in arid environments. Saline groundwater discharge cuts farm production, degrades natural environments and surface water, damages roads and leads to soil erosion. Restoring the balance needs deep-rooted vegetation such as mallee eucalyptus or perennial grasses, or farming adapted to shallow saline groundwater.

soil-chem-028.title: Australia's ancient salt, set loose by clearing
soil-chem-028.text: Australian soils have been gathering salt for thousands of years, from ocean winds, evaporated inland seas and weathered parent rocks. Before British settlement in 1788, groundwater levels were in equilibrium, because deep-rooted native vegetation used groundwater year-round. Land clearing replaced that vegetation with crops and pasture. Groundwater rose and brought the stored salt up, and evaporation left it in the soil. By 1999 about 2.5 million hectares had become salinized since European farming began. Some 5.7 million hectares now have high potential, a figure expected to reach 17 million by 2050. Most states are affected, above all south-west Western Australia, with around 70% of the country's salt-affected land. The causes differ by place: irrigation in the Murray River valley, land clearing near Werrimull in Victoria. Salt cuts plants' water uptake by osmosis, burns leaves through sodium and chloride and upsets nutrient balance. It also damages roads, buildings, pipes and cables. Predictions for climate change are mixed. Lower rainfall may reduce salinity, but heavier downpours may add excess water to aquifers.

soil-chem-017.title: Sodium adsorption ratio: a number for clay's stability
soil-chem-017.text: Sodium and calcium pull clay in opposite directions. Sodium and potassium disperse clay particles, while calcium and magnesium flocculate them into clumps. The sodium adsorption ratio, or SAR, weighs one side against the other. It is an irrigation water quality index calculated from sodium, calcium and magnesium concentrations: SAR = [Na+]/√([Ca2+]/2 + [Mg2+]/2), in milliequivalents per liter. Measured on pore water extracted from the soil, it is also the standard diagnostic of a soil's sodicity hazard. Below an SAR of 3 there is no problem. Above 9, fine-textured soils have severe problems, while sandy soils suffer less. For irrigation, SAR should not be much above 20, and preferably below 10. The damage builds slowly. Years of high-SAR water let sodium displace soil calcium and magnesium, ruining aggregate stability, structure and tilth and reducing infiltration and permeability. After long exposure, a soil's {{ref:soil-chem-018}} comes to roughly equal the water's SAR. SAR addresses sodium only. The potassium adsorption ratio (PAR) and the cation ratio of structural stability (CROSS) extend it to other cations.

soil-chem-030.title: Acid sulfate soils, harmless until they meet air
soil-chem-030.text: Left undisturbed below the water table, acid sulfate soils are benign. Drain them, dig them up or expose them to air, and their sulfides react with oxygen to form sulfuric acid. These are soils, sediments or organic substrates such as {{ref:soil-class-070}}, formed under waterlogged conditions, that contain iron sulfide minerals, mainly pyrite, or their oxidation products. Drained, they can turn extremely acidic, below pH 4. The acid releases iron, aluminium and other metals and metalloids, particularly arsenic. Together these kill vegetation and fish, acidify groundwater and surface water, and degrade concrete and steel structures to the point of failure. The most prone formed within the last 10,000 years. Then the last major sea level rise mixed seawater sulfate with land sediments rich in iron oxides and organic matter. They are widespread around coasts. In Australia, coastal acid sulfate soils cover an estimated 58,000 km2 beneath estuaries and floodplains. Canal, housing and marina works often disturb them, and droughts can expose them too. Some drained 100 years ago still release acid. Potential acid sulfate soils, or cat-clays, are often left uncultivated or planted with rice to keep them wet. The term was coined for the first International Symposium on Acid Sulfate Soils, held in 1972 at Wageningen.

soil-chem-012.title: Measuring salt by the current soil water carries
soil-chem-012.text: Seawater may hold 30 g/L of salt, or 3%, and has an electric conductivity of 50 dS/m. Soil salinity is measured on the same two scales: the salt concentration of the soil solution in g/L, or its electric conductivity (EC) in dS/m. The units relate by about 5/3, so y g/L corresponds to 5y/3 dS/m. The standard is the EC of an extract of a saturated soil paste, obtained by centrifugation and written ECe. A 2:1 or 5:1 water:soil mixture is easier to measure, and ECe is about 4 times the EC of a 2:1 mixture. Soils are saline when ECe exceeds 4. They are slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, and severely saline above 16. Sensitive crops already lose vigor in slightly saline soils. Most crops suffer in moderately saline ones, and only salt-resistant crops thrive in severely saline soils.

soil-chem-004.title: Rocks that leave acid soils behind
soil-chem-004.text: Some soils are acid from the start because of the rock beneath them. Acidic parent materials are rocks and sediments whose weathering acidifies the soils formed on them. Granites and allied igneous rocks are called 'acidic' because their abundant free quartz yields silicic acid on weathering. They are also low in calcium and magnesium. Sulfide-rich shale and coal, when hydrated and oxidized, produce sulfuric acid, much stronger than silicic acid. Many coal soils are too acidic for vigorous plant growth. Marine clays are often sulfide-rich and become very acidic if drained to an oxidizing state.

soil-chem-003.title: How roots and fallen needles acidify soil
soil-chem-003.text: Plant roots release protons and organic acids to chemically weather soil minerals. That is one face of biological acidification, the acidifying of soil by living things. Decaying plant remains add to it. Litter acidifies the O horizon more under conifers such as pine, spruce and fir, which return fewer base cations than deciduous trees. Cause and effect are tangled, though, since such pH differences often existed before the vegetation. Calcium held in living biomass also strongly affects soil pH, by an amount that varies between species.

soil-chem-006.title: What acid soil does to roots and life
soil-chem-006.text: In acid soil, roots come up short. Plants develop smaller, less durable roots with damaged tips, along with reduced height, poorer germination and stunted growth overall. Much of the harm traces to {{ref:soil-found-019}}. Leaching of base cations raises the availability of toxic ions such as aluminium, which inhibits root growth. Acidification also reduces the diversity of microbes and of larger creatures living in soil, and it is directly linked to declines in endangered plant species. Leaves yellowing between the veins can signal it, though alkaline or nutrient-poor soils cause the same symptom. At large scale, it cuts agricultural productivity.

soil-chem-007.title: Lime and careful habits against acid soil
soil-chem-007.text: {{ref:soil-fert-055}} of acidic soils under sugarcane, soybean and corn restored nutrients, raised pH, increased root biomass and improved plant health. Lime is the chief way to prevent or reverse soil acidification, alongside organic amendments, {{ref:soil-fert-050}} and careful fertilizer and irrigation management. Working lime in deeper works better than spreading it on the surface, but it is costlier and harder. Prevention starts with less acidifying fertilizers, timed so less nitrate washes out of the soil. Irrigating with acid-neutralizing water helps, as does weighing basic nutrients against the nitrogen removed in crops. Sulfur fertilizers belong only on responsive crops with a high rate of crop recovery.
